title.official: Judgment for debt or liquidated demand

division.heading: Actions Started by Statement of Claim

operative_text.controlling:
3.39(1)  If a statement of claim includes a claim for a debt or a
liquidated demand, with or without interest, whether as debt or
damages, and one or more defendants do not file a statement of
defence or demand for notice in response to that claim or any part
of it, the plaintiff
(a) may enter judgment for a sum not exceeding the amount
in respect of which no defence is filed and the interest
payable, if the interest calculation is based on a set rate,
either under an agreement or an enactment, and
(b) is entitled to a costs award.
(2)  In this rule, “liquidated demand” means
(a) a claim for a specific sum payable under an express or
implied contract for the payment of money, including
interest, not being in the nature of a penalty or
unliquidated damages, where the amount of money
claimed can be determined by
(i) the terms of the contract,
(ii) calculation only, or
(iii) taking an account between the plaintiff and the
defendant,
or
(b) a claim for a specific sum of money, whether or not in the
nature of a penalty or damages, recoverable under an
enactment that contains an express provision that the sum
that is the subject of the claim may be recovered as a
liquidated demand or as liquidated damages.

(c)Facts and Evidence Prejudgment interest should be based on evidence. So should any denial of interest because of the plaintiff's delay. The Court can award prejudgment interest higher than is named in the Judgment Interest Act, but that would need proof of loss of investment revenue, an agreement

for compound interest, or impropriety or bad faith. If a contract or bill of exchange gives a rate of interest, that usually applies, not the statutory prejudgment interest rate. Prejudgment interest applies to special damages also. If a contract is silent as to interest, but the court finds the

circumstances imply a term as to interest, in a commercial transaction it may be at a commercial rate, which was taken to be that in s.4(2) of theJudgment Interest Act. (d)When Interest Starts and Ends Prejudgment interest is to be calculated from the date that the cause of action arose.

Prejudgment interest for negligent misrepresentation or advice, only runs from when the damage accrues. If the suit is On when to begin calculating interest on a loan, see theMatthisoncase. for breach of contract, it runs from the date of breach. Where damages are assessed as of date of judgment, there is no reason to award pre-

judgment interest. Prejudgment interest is usually awarded only on the part of the damages which accrued up to the date of judgment.There cannot be prejudgment interest on pecuniary loss identified as arising after judgment, such as loss of capacity to earn in future. And if post- judgment interest is at a different rate, the court must calculate it on each part of the damages,

even before any overlap between the different heads of damage is deducted. Past lost earning capacity may be treated as a lost even stream of income, with interest calculated at 6-month intervals. If the breach continued or grew for some time, the amount owing may be calculated as of each January 1.

that the parties agreed on compound interest or knew that it was necessary.Royalty payments may typically be made over a long time and people may gain such rights as an investment, but it would take evidence of that, and a judge is not bound to take judicial notice of that and therefore

award compound interest. (h) Miscellaneous

A renewed judgment cannot capitalize interest in the old judgment, as that would lead to compound interest? Though statute allows prejudgment interest, the plaintiff normally should include a request for that in its pleadings, though a late amendment to do that may be possible.A request for such an

amendment is not hopeless if the evidence already before the court supports such an interest award. Where local legislation gives a discount rate to calculate damages as a lump sum, it applies in all cases, and cannot be adjusted for investment expenses, nor for the trial judge's idea of what the actual rate of return on investments would be.A damages award is to be final, and the trial

judge should not later adjust it to reflect what the plaintiff has spent a portion of the damages upon. commentary.text: Rule 3.39 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 3.39. 1. Interest Section 14(1) of the Judicature Act, R.S.A. 2000, c. J-2 permits the court to award interest “when in the opinion of the Court the payment of a just debt has been improperly withheld and it seems to the Court fair and equitable that the party in default should make compensation by the payment of interest …” 2. Test #1: “Just Debt” … the amount due to be a “just debt” must at least be ascertainable, though not necessarily precisely so, by reference to a contract or agreement between the parties and not as damages. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd. (1982), 20 Alta. L.R. (2d) 270 at 275 (C.A.). 3. Test #2: “Improperly Withheld” and “Fair and Equitable” Assuming this test [Test #1] to be satisfied, there still remains for decision the question of whether the just debt has been “improperly withheld” and whether it is “fair and equitable that” that interest be paid… In short, there must be something improper about the failure to pay the debt beyond the mere fact that it is due and not paid. So, in the case of one who did not have the means to pay, the failure to pay could hardly be regarded as “improper”. Cases where a failure to pay is nothing more than a deliberate attempt to reap the benefit of high interest rates or to put economic pressure on the creditor so as to induce him to take for immediate payment a sum less than he might otherwise receive may well be regarded as examples of an improper withholding of a just debt and where it is fair and reasonable that the creditor receive appropriate interest. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd., supra, at 275. 4. Practice Note (1) That interest should be claimed in the prayer for relief. (2) That in the body of a statement of claim the facts should be pleaded which establish that a just debt has been improperly withheld, giving such particulars as desirable, and that it is fair and equitable that the party in default should make compensation by payment of interest. (3) That it is desirable that the party claiming interest assert the basis for the rate of interest, such as alleging that a certain rate was his cost of borrowing, or, alternatively, that a certain rate was a return that would have been received by him had he been able to invest the money. Eyben v. K.R. Ranches (1970) Ltd., supra, at 275. With respect to (3), remember Kidd J.'s words in Renaissance Resources Ltd. v. Metalore Resources Ltd. (1984), 31 Alta. L.R. (2d) 226 (Q.B.), at 242: It is not sufficient for a plaintiff merely to indicate what bank he uses and what the prime interest rate of the bank is for the period the plaintiff is claiming interest … There must be some evidence of what it cost this plaintiff to borrow and whether he indeed had to borrow. If he did not have to borrow, evidence should be submitted as to the “return that would have been received by him had he been able to invest the money.” 5. Which Forum? For interest under the Judicature Act, one must seek the relief from a judge. That is clearly a claim for interest under s. 15 of the Judicature Act. That kind of claim is an unliquidated damage claim … Masters in Chambers do not have jurisdiction to grant such claims. Elgert Fertilizers Ltd. v. Schmitz (1985), 36 Alta. L.R. (2d) 327 (Master), at 329, per Master Funduk. 6. Implied Abandonment of s. 14 Judicature Act Claim I conclude that when a plaintiff is applying for summary judgment to a master in chambers, where the statement advances a claim for interest under s. 15 [now s. 14], that the plaintiff is abandoning that part of the claim. Elgert Fertilizers Ltd. v. Schmitz, supra, at 330.

BOOK_C.title: Judgment for debt or liquidated demand
BOOK_C.division_heading: Division 3 – ACTIONS STARTED BY STATEMENT OF CLAIM
BOOK_C.operative_text_raw:
(1) If a statement of claim includes a claim for a debt or a liquidated demand, with or without interest, whether as debt or damages, and one or more defendants do not file a statement of defence or demand for notice in response to that claim or any part of it, the plaintiff (a) may enter judgment for a sum not exceeding the amount in respect of which no defence is filed and the interest payable, if the interest calculation is based on a set rate, either under an agreement or an enactment, and (b) is entitled to a costs award.
(2) In this rule, “liquidated demand” means (a) a claim for a specific sum payable under an express or implied contract for the payment of money, including interest, not being in the nature of a penalty or unliquidated damages, where the amount of money claimed can be determined by (i) the terms of the contract, (ii) calculation only, or (iii) taking an account between the plaintiff and the defendant, or (b) a claim for a specific sum of money, whether or not in the nature of a penalty or damages, recoverable under an enactment that contains R. 3.39

commentary.text:
This rule permits the court (through the court clerk) to issue judgment for a debt or liquidated demand. This rule must be strictly complied with, or the court will refuse to enter judgment. See , [2015] A.J. No. 1092, 2015 ABQB 629 (Alta. Q.B.). Re Boisjoli This requires the pleadings in the statement of claim and the default judgment itself to comply. See , [2015] A.J. No. 1092, 2015 ABQB 629 (Alta. Q.B.). Re Boisjoli Interest, if claimed, must be specifically calculated in a schedule to the default judgment.
Under rule 3.39, default judgment is only available when the plaintiff sues for an exact, or easily calculable, amount. TLA Food Services Ltd. v. 1144707 Alberta Ltd., [2011] A.J. No. 975, 2011 ABQB 550 at para. For this reason, the statement of claim must be drafted very carefully, especially particulars of relief claimed, to enable the clerk to issue a default judgment as a mere clerical function, based only on the statement of claim and rudimentary calculations. If default judgment is refused, a plaintiff may still note the defendant in default pursuant to rule 3.36.
Judgment Against One Defendant Where Multiple Defendants – Rules 3.39 and 3.40 provide that where two parties are jointly liable and both are sued in one action but only one defends, the plaintiff may take default judgment and continue against the other. When this happens, the result (assuming the defended claim is successful in the end) is that there will be different judgments for different amounts, because contractual interest would continue to run against one debtor who defended but would stop as against the one against whom default proceedings were taken. On the defendant against whom default judgment is taken, interest thereafter accrues only under the Judgment Interest Act. Judgment Interest Act Domenic Construction Ltd. v. Primewest Capital , R.S.A. 2000, c. J-1; Corp., [2019] A.J. No. 108, 2019 ABQB 58 at para. 80 (Alta. Q.B.), revd (in part) on other grounds
